claim: The medial amygdala (MeA) occupies a central position in the vomeronasal pathway, upstream of hypothalamic centers dedicated to defensive and social responses.
source: The medial amygdala (MeA) occupies a central position in the vomeronasal pathway, upstream of hypothalamic centers dedicated to defensive and social responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical position and connectivity of the MeA within the vomeronasal pathway, drawing on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The MeA displays a degree of stimulus selectivity that is not observed in the upstream relay of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
source: In particular, we show that the MeA displays a degree of stimulus selectivity and a striking sexually dimorphic sensory representation that are not observed in the upstream relay of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing response selectivity between MeA and AOB neurons presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MeA displays a striking sexually dimorphic sensory representation that is not observed in the upstream relay of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
source: In particular, we show that the MeA displays a degree of stimulus selectivity and a striking sexually dimorphic sensory representation that are not observed in the upstream relay of the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing male and female responses in MeA versus AOB presented in the manuscript.

claim: The development of sexually dimorphic circuits in the MeA requires steroid signaling near the time of puberty to organize the functional representation of sensory stimuli.
source: Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the development of sexually dimorphic circuits in the MeA requires steroid signaling near the time of puberty to organize the functional representation of sensory stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from juvenile mice, aromatase knockout mice, and estrogen-treated mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: Impairment in either vomeronasal or olfactory signaling results in dramatic deficits in predator avoidance and social communication.
source: Impairment in either vomeronasal or olfactory signaling results in dramatic deficits in predator avoidance and social communication (Bean and Wysocki, 1989; Stowers et al., 2002; Mandiyan et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2005; Kimchi et al., 2007; Kobayakawa et al., 2007; Isogai et al., 2011), demonstrating that chemical cues are essential mediators of animal–animal recognition in mice and that the main olfactory system and the vomeronasal pathway work in concert to guide behavioral responses to chemosensory input (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Dulac and Kimchi 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: Chemical cues are essential mediators of animal–animal recognition in mice.
source: Impairment in either vomeronasal or olfactory signaling results in dramatic deficits in predator avoidance and social communication (Bean and Wysocki, 1989; Stowers et al., 2002; Mandiyan et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2005; Kimchi et al., 2007; Kobayakawa et al., 2007; Isogai et al., 2011), demonstrating that chemical cues are essential mediators of animal–animal recognition in mice and that the main olfactory system and the vomeronasal pathway work in concert to guide behavioral responses to chemosensory input (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Dulac and Kimchi 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies showing deficits when chemosensory signaling is impaired.

claim: The main olfactory system and the vomeronasal pathway work in concert to guide behavioral responses to chemosensory input.
source: Impairment in either vomeronasal or olfactory signaling results in dramatic deficits in predator avoidance and social communication (Bean and Wysocki, 1989; Stowers et al., 2002; Mandiyan et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2005; Kimchi et al., 2007; Kobayakawa et al., 2007; Isogai et al., 2011), demonstrating that chemical cues are essential mediators of animal–animal recognition in mice and that the main olfactory system and the vomeronasal pathway work in concert to guide behavioral responses to chemosensory input (Dulac and Wagner, 2006; Dulac and Kimchi 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Volatile compounds are primarily detected by the MOE while non-volatile signals are preferentially processed by the VNO.
source: The main olfactory epithelium (MOE) and vomeronasal organ (VNO) are distinguished by the types of chemical cues that each detects: volatile compounds are primarily detected by the MOE while non-volatile signals are preferentially processed by the VNO.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the functional specialization of these two chemosensory systems.

claim: Neurons in the MOE project to the main olfactory bulb (MOB), which in turn projects axons to the lateral amygdala, primary olfactory cortex, and ultimately to areas involved in the cognitive processing of odorants.
source: At the circuit level, neurons in the MOE project to the main olfactory bulb (MOB), which in turn projects axons to the lateral amygdala, primary olfactory cortex, and ultimately to areas involved in the cognitive processing of odorants (Sosulski et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim describes the anatomical connectivity of the main olfactory pathway and is supported by a citation.

claim: Sensory neurons of the VNO send axons to the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB), which in turn projects to nuclei of the medial amygdala (MeA), the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the hypothalamus.
source: In contrast, vomeronasal circuits largely bypass cognitive centers, as sensory neurons of the VNO send axons to the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB), which in turn projects to nuclei of the medial amygdala (MeA), the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the hypothalamus (Petrovich et al., 2001), areas involved in controlling innate behaviors and neuroendocrine changes.
evidence: This claim describes the anatomical connectivity of the vomeronasal pathway and is supported by a citation.

claim: Vomeronasal circuits largely bypass cognitive centers.
source: In contrast, vomeronasal circuits largely bypass cognitive centers, as sensory neurons of the VNO send axons to the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB), which in turn projects to nuclei of the medial amygdala (MeA), the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the hypothalamus (Petrovich et al., 2001), areas involved in controlling innate behaviors and neuroendocrine changes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anatomical connectivity pattern described and cited.

claim: The MeA, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and hypothalamus are areas involved in controlling innate behaviors and neuroendocrine changes.
source: In contrast, vomeronasal circuits largely bypass cognitive centers, as sensory neurons of the VNO send axons to the accessory olfactory bulb (AOB), which in turn projects to nuclei of the medial amygdala (MeA), the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the hypothalamus (Petrovich et al., 2001), areas involved in controlling innate behaviors and neuroendocrine changes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the function of these brain regions.

claim: Distinct populations of VNO receptors identify ethologically relevant chemosignals with high specificity.
source: In vitro recording and imaging of VNO neuronal activity after exposure to various stimuli, as well as in vivo characterization of the vomeronasal receptor response profile to a wide range of animal cues, have revealed that distinct populations of VNO receptors identify ethologically relevant chemosignals with high specificity and that signal detection in the VNO plays an essential role in distinguishing behaviorally relevant sensory information (Holy et al., 2000; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2000; Nodari et al., 2008; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2009; Haga et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2011; Turaga and Holy, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: Signal detection in the VNO plays an essential role in distinguishing behaviorally relevant sensory information.
source: In vitro recording and imaging of VNO neuronal activity after exposure to various stimuli, as well as in vivo characterization of the vomeronasal receptor response profile to a wide range of animal cues, have revealed that distinct populations of VNO receptors identify ethologically relevant chemosignals with high specificity and that signal detection in the VNO plays an essential role in distinguishing behaviorally relevant sensory information (Holy et al., 2000; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2000; Nodari et al., 2008; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2009; Haga et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2011; Turaga and Holy, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: A large proportion of output neurons in the AOB respond to multiple classes of stimuli.
source: In contrast to the apparent specificity of VNO responses for distinct animal cues, a large proportion of output neurons in the AOB, the primary targets of VNO sensory projections, were shown to respond to multiple classes of stimuli (Luo et al., 2003; Hendrickson et al., 2008; Ben-Shaul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Many AOB mitral/tufted cells respond with similar strength to cues such as female and predator odors, which are clearly associated with opposing behavioral outcomes.
source: In particular, many AOB mitral/tufted cells respond with similar strength to cues such as female and predator odors, which are clearly associated with opposing behavioral outcomes (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: The complex responses of AOB mitral/tufted cells, together with their distinctive multi-branched dendritic trees, suggest that they integrate sensory information across distinct vomeronasal receptors.
source: The complex responses of AOB mitral/tufted cells, together with their distinctive multi-branched dendritic trees, suggest that they integrate sensory information across distinct vomeronasal receptors (Wagner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed response properties and anatomical features, supported by a citation.

claim: Downstream vomeronasal centers that control behavioral outputs must be able to interpret and disambiguate the relevant information from broad patterns of AOB activity.
source: Ultimately, downstream vomeronasal centers that control behavioral outputs must be able to interpret and disambiguate the relevant information from these broad patterns of AOB activity.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that AOB neurons respond broadly while behaviors are specific.

claim: The MeA is the primary recipient of AOB inputs.
source: The MeA is the primary recipient of AOB inputs, it projects to distinct nuclei of the hypothalamus involved in social and defensive responses (Petrovich et al., 2001; Choi et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2011) and disruptions in MeA signaling cause profound deficits in social and predator recognition (Ferguson et al., 2001; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The MeA projects to distinct nuclei of the hypothalamus involved in social and defensive responses.
source: The MeA is the primary recipient of AOB inputs, it projects to distinct nuclei of the hypothalamus involved in social and defensive responses (Petrovich et al., 2001; Choi et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2011) and disruptions in MeA signaling cause profound deficits in social and predator recognition (Ferguson et al., 2001; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Disruptions in MeA signaling cause profound deficits in social and predator recognition.
source: The MeA is the primary recipient of AOB inputs, it projects to distinct nuclei of the hypothalamus involved in social and defensive responses (Petrovich et al., 2001; Choi et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2011) and disruptions in MeA signaling cause profound deficits in social and predator recognition (Ferguson et al., 2001; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: MeA units responsive to sensory stimuli were localized to the ventral surface of the brain and extended approximately 1 mm dorsally, consistent with the anatomy of the posterior MeA.
source: MeA units responsive to sensory stimuli were localized to the ventral surface of the brain and extended approximately 1 mm dorsally, consistent with the anatomy of the posterior MeA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the recordings.

claim: 197 units (82 single units; 115 multi units) recorded from the MeA of 55 adult BALB/c mice responded to sensory stimuli (p<0.01, non-parametric ANOVA).
source: In this study, 197 units (82 single units; 115 multi units) recorded from the MeA of 55 adult BALB/c mice (10–12 weeks old; sexually naive) responded to sensory stimuli (p<0.01, non-parametric ANOVA).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Baseline firing rates of single MeA units were typically very low (0.21 ± 0.02 Hz).
source: Baseline firing rates of single MeA units were typically very low (0.21 ± 0.02 Hz; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and referenced figure.

claim: Upon VNO stimulation, MeA units responded in stimulus-locked and stimulus-specific manner that resembled sensory responses observed in the AOB in both latency and duration.
source: Upon VNO stimulation, MeA units responded in stimulus-locked and stimulus-specific manner (Figure 1C) that resembled sensory responses observed in the AOB in both latency and duration (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and comparison to a cited study.

claim: MeA units typically increased their firing rate after a preferred stimulus was presented reaching a peak firing rate (8.1 ± 0.31 Hz) ∼5 s after stimulus presentation.
source: MeA units typically increased their firing rate after a preferred stimulus was presented reaching a peak firing rate (8.1 ± 0.31 Hz) ∼5 s after stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collected in the study.

claim: MOE stimulation elicited clear olfactory-evoked neuronal activity in the MOB and the posterolateral cortical amygdala (PLCO) in response to volatile urinary cues and odorants.
source: MOE stimulation elicited clear olfactory-evoked neuronal activity in the MOB and the posterolateral cortical amygdala (PLCO) in response to volatile urinary cues and odorants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Robust VNO-mediated responses were observed in the MeA, but stimulus-specific responses for MOE-delivered stimuli were not detected.
source: However, while we observed robust VNO-mediated responses in the MeA, we did not detect stimulus-specific responses for MOE-delivered stimuli (units responsive to MOE stimuli at p≤0.01: 1.1%, 95% CI: 0.8–1.6%; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text and Figure 1D.

claim: There is little evidence that distinct volatile stimuli elicit specific sensory responses in the MeA.
source: Rather, in agreement with Samuelsen and Meredith (2009) and Miyamichi et al. (2011), we found little evidence that distinct volatile stimuli elicit specific sensory responses in the MeA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations and agreement with cited studies.

claim: The vomeronasal system emerged as the dominant sensory input to the MeA units recorded.
source: Therefore, the vomeronasal system emerged as the dominant sensory input to the MeA units we recorded.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing strong VNO responses and weak MOE responses.

claim: FluoroGold retrogradely labeled ∼100 times more AOB than MOB neurons.
source: However, we found that FluoroGold retrogradely labeled ∼100 times more AOB than MOB neurons, clearly demonstrating the dominance of AOB inputs, especially in light of the much larger number of MOB compared to AOB neurons (Figure 1F,G; see Miyamichi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Functional and anatomical evidence confirms that the MeA, as targeted in these experiments, receives input predominantly from the AOB.
source: Therefore, functional and anatomical evidence confirms that the MeA, as targeted in these experiments, receives input predominantly from the AOB (Pro-sistiaga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Vomeronasal sensory responses of MeA units typically exhibited high specificity for one stimulus or a subset of the tested stimuli.
source: Sensory responses of MeA units typically exhibited high specificity for one stimulus or a subset of the tested stimuli (Figure 2), with a smaller number of MeA units responding broadly to multiple stimuli from both conspecific and non-conspecific sources (Figure 2, bottom four rows).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A clear topographical segregation of sensory responses is apparent in the real time response properties of MeA units.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we found that a clear topographical segregation of sensory responses is apparent in the real time response properties of MeA units.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations consistent with previous research.

claim: Neurons that responded most strongly to 'conspecific' stimuli were typically located dorsal to neurons that responded most strongly to 'predator' stimuli.
source: Neurons that responded most strongly to 'conspecific' stimuli were typically located dorsal to neurons that responded most strongly to 'predator' stimuli, and this was true for data recorded from male or female animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MeA neurons that responded significantly to multiple stimuli with varying response strengths were observed, indicating that individual neurons distributed throughout the MeA have access to information about both conspecific and defensive stimuli.
source: However, we also observed MeA neurons that responded significantly to multiple stimuli with varying response strengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that individual neurons distributed throughout the MeA have access to information about both conspecific and defensive stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The percentage of units responding to each stimulus is dramatically lower in the MeA than it is in the AOB.
source: Thus, the percentage of units responding to each stimulus is dramatically lower in the MeA than it is in the AOB (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing AOB and MeA responses shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparison of the response distributions between the AOB and the MeA reveals a clear and significant shift to values with higher selectivity in the MeA (p<0.0001; permutation test).
source: Comparison of the response distributions between the AOB and the MeA reveals a clear and significant shift to values with higher selectivity in the MeA (Figure 3B; p<0.0001; permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 44.4% of AOB units vs 21.6% of MeA units reside in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses.
source: Dividing the triangular response space into four equal quadrants (dashed lines Figure 3C,D) showed that 44.4% of AOB units vs 21.6% of MeA units reside in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Flow of information from the AOB to the MeA is associated with a sharpening of stimulus-driven responses.
source: Thus, flow of information from the AOB to the MeA is associated with a sharpening of stimulus-driven responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing increased selectivity in MeA compared to AOB.

claim: The increased selectivity of sensory responses in the MeA is reflected by a marked decorrelation of responses evoked by different sensory stimuli across the MeA population.
source: The increased selectivity of sensory responses in the MeA is similarly reflected by a marked decorrelation of responses evoked by different sensory stimuli across the MeA population (AOB: Figure 3C inset; MeA: Figure 3D inset; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The first principal component reflected the distinction between 'female' and 'predator' categories and accounted for 41% of the total response variance.
source: A principal component analysis performed on responses evoked by these stimuli revealed that the first PC reflected the distinction between 'female' and 'predator' categories and accounted for 41% of the total response variance (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component analysis of experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The second principal component distinguished between 'female' vs 'male' stimuli and accounted for 19% of the total variance.
source: The second PC distinguished between 'female' vs 'male' stimuli and accounted for 19% of the total variance.
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component analysis of experimental data.

claim: Most of the variation of sensory responses in the MeA of male mice is devoted to the distinction between 'female' from 'predator' and 'male' categories respectively.
source: Therefore, most of the variation of sensory responses in the MeA of male mice is devoted to the distinction between 'female' from 'predator' and 'male' categories respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the principal component analysis results.

claim: Individual sensory responses in the MeA rarely form sharply defined stimulus categories, but rather, maintain enough information to distinguish between individual elements of each category.
source: However, individual sensory responses in the MeA rarely form sharply defined stimulus categories, but rather, maintain enough information to distinguish between individual elements of each category (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: MeA responses are dramatically more frequent to opposite-sex stimuli.
source: This analysis revealed a striking sexual dimorphism in the stimulus selectivity of MeA units (Figure 4B), such that MeA responses are dramatically more frequent to opposite-sex stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing male and female MeA responses shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 82.7% of male MeA units respond more strongly to female stimuli and 83.3% of female MeA units respond stronger to male stimuli.
source: Indeed, 82.7% of male MeA units respond more strongly to female stimuli and 83.3% of female MeA units respond stronger to male stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: For both sexes, there is an unmistakable overrepresentation of responses to stimuli from the opposite sex.
source: Thus, for both sexes, there is an unmistakable overrepresentation of responses to stimuli from the opposite sex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: The ratio of predator to conspecific responsive units was significantly higher in the MeA of female vs male mice.
source: In addition, the ratio of predator to conspecific responsive units was significantly higher in the MeA of female vs male mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The responses of AOB units recorded from both male and female animals share a moderate bias in responses for female stimuli.
source: Rather, the responses of AOB units recorded from both male and female animals share a moderate bias in responses for female stimuli (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The profound sexual dimorphism of sensory representations is an emergent property of the MeA.
source: Thus, the profound sexual dimorphism of sensory representations described here is an emergent property of the MeA.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the comparison of AOB and MeA responses in males and females.

claim: Single units recorded from the MeA of juvenile mice responded to VNO stimuli, but were far less selective for male, female, and predator cues than those in the adult MeA.
source: We found that, while single units recorded from the MeA of juvenile mice responded to VNO stimuli, they were far less selective for male, female, and predator cues (Figure 4C,F) than those in the adult MeA (Figure 4B,E), and instead showed closer similarity with the response selectivity identified in the adult AOB (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing juvenile and adult MeA responses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 34.7% of juvenile units were in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses, as opposed to 21.6% in the adult MeA.
source: Thus, 34.7% of juvenile units were in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses, as opposed to 21.6% in the adult MeA.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data comparing juvenile and adult MeA responses.

claim: The selectivity of MeA responses to opposite sex cues is absent in juvenile animals, and was not significantly different between males and females (p=0.06, permutation test).
source: The selectivity of MeA responses to opposite sex cues is absent in juvenile animals, and was not significantly different between males and females (Figure 4F; p=0.06, permutation test), a feature also shared with the adult AOB and strikingly different from the adult MeA.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: MeA responses in juvenile mice are not sexually dimorphic.
source: Thus, MeA responses in juvenile mice are not sexually dimorphic, even though the perinatal organizational phase of MeA sexual development, during which steroid-dependent cell death generates sexually dimorphic MeA cell numbers, is essentially complete (Wu et al., 2009), and appear instead highly reminiscent to the responses observed in the AOB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and comparison to cited research.

claim: The MeApd is a primary site of aromatase expression.
source: Although sparse in the rodent brain, the MeApd is a primary site of aromatase expression, and sexual dimorphisms in MeA regional volume, cell number, and neural connectivity are mediated by aromatase-dependent sex-steroid signaling (see Cooke et al., 1999; McCarthy, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sexual dimorphisms in MeA regional volume, cell number, and neural connectivity are mediated by aromatase-dependent sex-steroid signaling.
source: Although sparse in the rodent brain, the MeApd is a primary site of aromatase expression, and sexual dimorphisms in MeA regional volume, cell number, and neural connectivity are mediated by aromatase-dependent sex-steroid signaling (see Cooke et al., 1999; McCarthy, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MeA units from ArKO−/− males frequently responded to multiple stimuli.
source: As predicted, MeA units from ArKO−/− males frequently responded to multiple stimuli; whereas, MeA units from age matched heterozygous littermates (ArKO+/−) were similar to those observed in wild-type males (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The sex specificity of neurons recorded in adult ArKO−/− males is largely symmetric around 0, and presents a pattern of responses intermediate to those observed in intact juvenile and adult male mice.
source: Indeed, the sex specificity of neurons recorded in adult ArKO−/− males is largely symmetric around 0, and presents a pattern of responses intermediate to those observed in intact juvenile and adult male mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Most (42.1%) of MeA units recorded from adult ArKO−/− males reside in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses, compared to 19.5% of units recorded from ArKO+/−.
source: Like juvenile animals, most (42.1%) of MeA units recorded from adult ArKO−/− males reside in the central quadrant associated with less specific responses, compared to 19.5% of units recorded from ArKO+/−.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data comparing ArKO−/− and ArKO+/− mice.

claim: Response patterns to different stimuli are much more correlated in the MeA of ArKO−/− males than in ArKO+/− littermates or wild-type males, reflecting a loss of discriminability at the individual unit level.
source: Similarly, response patterns to different stimuli are much more correlated in the MeA of ArKO−/− males (Figure 5C, bottom) than in ArKO+/− littermates (Figure 5C, top) or wild-type males (Figure 3D), reflecting a loss of discriminability at the individual unit level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Estrogen signaling (via conversion of testosterone by aromatase) is essential for generating the pattern of sensory responses observed in the adult male MeA.
source: These results suggest that estrogen signaling (via conversion of testosterone by aromatase) is essential for generating the pattern of sensory responses observed in the adult male MeA.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data from ArKO mice.

claim: The fact that adult ArKO−/− males are also different from juvenile males indicates that other processes, such as direct testosterone signaling, may play an important role in developing the adult MeA sensory representation.
source: The fact that adult ArKO−/− males are also different from juvenile males indicates that other processes, such as direct testosterone signaling, may play an important role in developing the adult MeA sensory representation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the differences observed between ArKO−/− and juvenile mice.

claim: In estrogen treated females, 51.2% of MeA neurons respond more strongly to female than to male stimuli, with 26.7% responding to female stimuli at least 3 times stronger than to male stimuli.
source: However, in estrogen treated females, 51.2% of MeA neurons respond more strongly to female than to male stimuli, with 26.7% responding to female stimuli at least 3 times stronger than to male stimuli (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: This novel subset of neurons (female responsive in female animals) is located more dorsally relative to predator-responsive neurons, as is typical of female responsive neurons in males.
source: This novel subset of neurons (female responsive in female animals) is located more dorsally relative to predator-responsive neurons, as is typical of female responsive neurons in males (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Estrogen treatment resulted in a clear reduction of the number of neurons selective for male stimuli.
source: In addition, estrogen treatment resulted in a clear reduction of the number of neurons selective for male stimuli (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The fraction of MeA neurons responding to any given stimulus is smaller than in the AOB.
source: Nearly all AOB output neurons project to the MeA, however, the convergence of input in the MeA lead to a different pattern of sensory responses, such that the fraction of MeA neurons responding to any given stimulus is smaller, and the specificity of MeA responses elicited by sensory stimuli is greater than observed in the AOB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data comparing AOB and MeA responses.

claim: The specificity of MeA responses elicited by sensory stimuli is greater than observed in the AOB.
source: Nearly all AOB output neurons project to the MeA, however, the convergence of input in the MeA lead to a different pattern of sensory responses, such that the fraction of MeA neurons responding to any given stimulus is smaller, and the specificity of MeA responses elicited by sensory stimuli is greater than observed in the AOB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data comparing AOB and MeA responses.

claim: The low stimulus specificity observed in AOB responses is likely generated by the integration of VR inputs by individual AOB mitral cells.
source: Instead, the complex AOB representation we observe is likely generated by the integration of VR inputs by individual AOB mitral cells (Wagner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed response patterns and cited anatomical evidence.

claim: A general feature of sensory systems is that neurons located at later stages of sensory processing are less active than those at earlier stages.
source: A general feature of sensory systems is that neurons located at later stages of sensory processing are less active than those at earlier stages.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about sensory systems.

claim: Sparse coding at higher processing areas is well described in vision and olfaction, and is thought to reflect the construction of increasingly complex sensory representations.
source: Sparse coding at higher processing areas is well described in vision and olfaction (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Quiroga et al., 2005; Poo and Isaacson, 2009), and is thought to reflect the construction of increasingly complex sensory representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fraction of neurons activated by any given stimulus is approximately threefold greater in the AOB compared to the MeA.
source: Similarly, we find that the fraction of neurons activated by any given stimulus is approximately threefold greater in the AOB compared to the MeA.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on experimental data.

claim: MeA neurons of adult mice respond to vomeronasal stimuli with significantly more specificity for behaviorally distinct classes of stimuli than AOB neurons.
source: We also found that MeA neurons of adult mice respond to vomeronasal stimuli with significantly more specificity for behaviorally distinct classes of stimuli than AOB neurons, and the number of MeA neurons responding to behaviorally conflicting stimuli, although not absent, is lower than observed in the AOB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data comparing AOB and MeA responses.

claim: The number of MeA neurons responding to behaviorally conflicting stimuli, although not absent, is lower than observed in the AOB.
source: We also found that MeA neurons of adult mice respond to vomeronasal stimuli with significantly more specificity for behaviorally distinct classes of stimuli than AOB neurons, and the number of MeA neurons responding to behaviorally conflicting stimuli, although not absent, is lower than observed in the AOB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data comparing AOB and MeA responses.

claim: The complex responses typical of AOB neurons are interpreted by the MeA in a manner that promotes the emergence of sensory responses more closely associated with a specific behavioral output.
source: Thus, the complex responses typical of AOB neurons are interpreted by the MeA in a manner that promotes the emergence of sensory responses more closely associated with a specific behavioral output, and may help generate unambiguous and mutually exclusive behaviors (e.g.: aggression, courtship, parenting, or predator defense).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in response selectivity between AOB and MeA.

claim: The greater MeA selectivity may result from the preferential contribution of the most selective AOB units to MeA responses, or from the transformation of AOB inputs by sensory processing within the MeA.
source: The greater MeA selectivity may result from the preferential contribution of the most selective AOB units to MeA responses, or from the transformation of AOB inputs by sensory processing within the MeA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms underlying the observed selectivity.

claim: The apparent functional disambiguation of AOB inputs by MeA units suggests a logic and specificity in AOB to MeA connectivity that strongly contrasts with the distributive pattern of projection reported from the MOB to the piriform cortex.
source: The apparent functional disambiguation of AOB inputs by MeA units suggests a logic and specificity in AOB to MeA connectivity that strongly contrasts with the distributive pattern of projection reported from the MOB to the piriform cortex (Sosulski et al., 2011, Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed functional properties and comparison to cited research on MOB-piriform connectivity.

claim: MeA responses display a relatively long latency (several seconds) and slow time-course (tens of seconds) that is likely a direct result of the slow dynamics of large non-volatile sensory stimuli that activate VRs.
source: As observed in the VNO and AOB, MeA responses display a relatively long latency (several seconds) and slow time-course (tens of seconds) that is likely a direct result of the slow dynamics of large non-volatile sensory stimuli that activate VRs (Holy et al., 2000; Hendrickson et al., 2008; Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Shpak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed response properties and comparison to cited research.

claim: Nearly half of the neurons in this study were completely silent until a preferred sensory stimulus was presented.
source: Nearly half of the neurons in this study were completely silent until a preferred sensory stimulus was presented, and nearly all single-unit responses identified in this study consisted of stimulus-evoked increases in neural activity.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Nearly all single-unit responses identified in this study consisted of stimulus-evoked increases in neural activity.
source: Nearly half of the neurons in this study were completely silent until a preferred sensory stimulus was presented, and nearly all single-unit responses identified in this study consisted of stimulus-evoked increases in neural activity.

claim: c-Fos induction is observed in large subsets of MeA neurons following exposure of animals to reproductive and defensive stimuli.
source: This is consistent with c-Fos induction observed in large subsets of MeA neurons following exposure of animals to reproductive and defensive stimuli (Choi et al., 2005) and the strong monosynaptic excitatory input from AOB fibers on MeA neurons (Bian et al., 2008; Niimi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is strong monosynaptic excitatory input from AOB fibers on MeA neurons.
source: This is consistent with c-Fos induction observed in large subsets of MeA neurons following exposure of animals to reproductive and defensive stimuli (Choi et al., 2005) and the strong monosynaptic excitatory input from AOB fibers on MeA neurons (Bian et al., 2008; Niimi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible that the MeA functions differently in awake vs anesthetized animals.
source: Since the MeA receives a broad range of modulatory inputs from other brain regions and is likely to be affected by the animal's behavioral state, it is possible that the MeA functions differently in awake vs anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the anesthetized preparation.

claim: Sensory processing in the main olfactory system is clearly altered by anesthesia level and behavioral state.
source: Sensory processing in the main olfactory system is clearly altered by anesthesia level and behavioral state (Rinberg et al., 2006; Cazakoff et al., 2014), and relating the findings from the current study to data from behaving animals will be an important step for future studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Male and female moths (Manduca sexta) and silkworms (Bombyx mori) express an array of olfactory receptors that are not expressed by the opposite sex.
source: For example, male and female moths (Manduca sexta) and silkworms (Bombyx mori) express an array of olfactory receptors that are not expressed by the opposite sex (Hansson et al., 1989; Nakagawa et al., 2005; Große-Wilde et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Drosophila pheromone 11-cis Vaccenyl acetate (cVA) elicits sexually dimorphic behaviors, but the sensory neurons that detect cVA are anatomically and functionally indistinguishable in males and females.
source: For example, the Drosophila pheromone 11-cis Vaccenyl acetate (cVA) elicits sexually dimorphic behaviors, but the sensory neurons that detect cVA are anatomically and functionally indistinguishable in males and females (Kurtovic et al., 2007; Datta et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The influence of cVA on sexually dimorphic behaviors is achieved through differential projections of cVA input to the sexually dimorphic network of fru expressing neurons in the central nervous system.
source: Instead, the influence of cVA on sexually dimorphic behaviors is achieved through differential projections of cVA input to the sexually dimorphic network of fru expressing neurons in the central nervous system (Datta et al., 2008; Ruta et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The capacity for male, but not female, finches to sing is attributed to circuit differences in premotor nuclei.
source: Even more centrally based, the capacity for male, but not female, finches to sing is attributed to circuit differences in premotor nuclei (Nottebohm and Arnold, 1976; Konishi and Akutagawa, 1985; Kirn, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is little evidence for substantial differences in sensory responses of the male and female VNO or AOB.
source: However, although sexually dimorphic anatomical features have indeed long been identified at every stage of the vomeronasal pathway, including in the VNO, AOB, amygdala, and hypothalamic areas (Guillamón and Segovia, 1997), there is little evidence for substantial differences in sensory responses of the male and female VNO or AOB (Nodari et al., 2008; Herrada and Dulac, 1997; Kang et al., 2009; Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Haga et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Downstream circuits are likely to contribute significantly to generate, or amplify, sexually dimorphic sensory processing.
source: Thus, downstream circuits are likely to contribute significantly to generate, or amplify, sexually dimorphic sensory processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of sexual dimorphism in VNO/AOB and the presence of sexually dimorphic behaviors.

claim: Silencing the VNO, genetically or surgically, brings about a set of behaviors that are typically seen in the opposite sex.
source: Previous studies show that silencing the VNO, genetically or surgically, brings about a set of behaviors that are typically seen in the opposite sex (Stowers et al., 2002; Kimchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Effector circuits for behaviors of both sexes exist in the brain, and are activated or repressed by vomeronasal activity in a sex-specific manner.
source: These findings demonstrate the essential contribution of the vomeronasal system to the control of social behaviors, and show that effector circuits for behaviors of both sexes exist in the brain, and are activated or repressed by vomeronasal activity in a sex-specific manner (Kimchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited behavioral studies.

claim: The transformation of the vomeronasal sensory representation in the MeA precisely fulfills the characteristics required of a behavioral switch.
source: The transformation of the vomeronasal sensory representation in the MeA precisely fulfills the characteristics required of such a behavioral switch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing sexually dimorphic MeA responses.

claim: Over 80% of the recorded MeA neurons respond preferentially to stimuli from the opposite sex.
source: Unlike the AOB, in which sensory responses are similar in males and females, over 80% of the recorded MeA neurons respond preferentially to stimuli from the opposite sex.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: An entire category of 'same-sex' responses is decimated in the MeA representation.
source: Accordingly, an entire category of 'same-sex' responses is decimated in the MeA representation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing strong opposite-sex bias.

claim: The lack of male to male aggression in TRPC2−/− mice demonstrates that the representation of male stimuli, in male mice, is present in wild-type animals, depends on vomeronasal signaling, and is capable of driving robust behaviors.
source: Same-sex information is not entirely lost: indeed, the lack of male to male aggression in TRPC2−/− mice demonstrates that the representation of male stimuli, in male mice, is present in wild-type animals, depends on vomeronasal signaling, and is capable of driving robust behaviors (Stowers et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited behavioral studies in knockout mice.

claim: Same sex-information may either rely on the minimal representation found in the MeA, or be processed preferentially by other secondary vomeronasal relays.
source: Same sex-information may therefore either rely on the minimal representation found in the MeA, or be processed preferentially by other secondary vomeronasal relays.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms for processing same-sex information.

claim: It is generally believed that testosterone accounts for most, if not all, of development of the known sexually dimorphic structures in the mammalian brain.
source: It is generally believed that testosterone accounts for most, if not all, of development of the known sexually dimorphic structures in the mammalian brain (Morris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cell death, synapse formation, synapse elimination, neurogenesis, and changes to neuron morphology all play important roles in how testosterone shapes the nervous system.
source: The manner by which testosterone shapes the nervous system, however, depends on the specific neural circuit, such that cell death, synapse formation, synapse elimination, neurogenesis, and changes to neuron morphology all play important roles (Cooke et al., 1999; Ibanez et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2008; Forger & de Vries, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The MeA of mice is morphologically sexually dimorphic such that males have a larger posterodorsal MeA (MeApd) than females.
source: The MeA of mice is morphologically sexually dimorphic such that males have a larger posterodorsal MeA (MeApd) than females (Cooke et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2004), a difference primarily attributed to differential cell death at birth (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The size difference in MeApd between males and females is primarily attributed to differential cell death at birth.
source: The MeA of mice is morphologically sexually dimorphic such that males have a larger posterodorsal MeA (MeApd) than females (Cooke et al., 1999; Morris et al., 2004), a difference primarily attributed to differential cell death at birth (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Recordings from the MeA of mice in the week prior to puberty onset demonstrate that MeA units had not developed the sexually dimorphic response patterns characteristic of adult animals.
source: Our recordings from the MeA of mice in the week prior to puberty onset demonstrate that MeA units had not developed the sexually dimorphic response patterns characteristic of adult animals, although these recordings were performed after sex-specific cell death is largely complete (Wu et al., 2009; see ; Forger and de Vries, 2010).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental findings.

claim: The organizational phase of steroid-dependent MeA cell death likely provides a template for future sexually dimorphic sensory responses, but is not in itself sufficient to endow the MeA with adult function.
source: Therefore, the organizational phase of steroid-dependent MeA cell death likely provides a template for future sexually dimorphic sensory responses, but is not in itself sufficient to endow the MeA with adult function that might, for example, require further elimination of neurons with the wrong sex cue specificity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from juvenile mice.

claim: Juvenile MeA neurons are not silent but rather respond vigorously to vomeronasal stimuli in a manner very similar to AOB neurons in adult animals, demonstrating that the MeA is already an actively functioning circuit.
source: Importantly, juvenile MeA neurons are not silent but rather respond vigorously to vomeronasal stimuli in a manner very similar to AOB neurons in adult animals, demonstrating that the MeA is already an actively functioning circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from juvenile mice.

claim: A second phase of circuit organization is required to shape sex-specific responses in adults.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that a second phase of circuit organization is required to shape sex-specific responses in adults.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data comparing juvenile and adult mice.

claim: Recordings from animals with manipulated hormone levels and hormone signaling show that sexually dimorphic patterns of MeA function in adult mice are estrogen dependent.
source: Our recordings from animals with manipulated hormone levels and hormone signaling show that sexually dimorphic patterns of MeA function in adult mice are estrogen dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from ArKO mice and estrogen-treated mice.

claim: Previous experiments studying an independently made ArKO mouse line reported significant impairment in social recognition.
source: Previous experiments studying an independently made ArKO mouse line reported significant impairment in social recognition (Bakker et al., 2002), which may result from the failure of MeA neurons in ArKO animals to maturate adult patterns of MeA responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The impairment in social recognition in ArKO mice may result from the failure of MeA neurons in ArKO animals to maturate adult patterns of MeA responses.
source: Previous experiments studying an independently made ArKO mouse line reported significant impairment in social recognition (Bakker et al., 2002), which may result from the failure of MeA neurons in ArKO animals to maturate adult patterns of MeA responses.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the behavioral phenotype to the observed neural phenotype.

claim: In some species of mammals, the influence of sex-steroids on MeA anatomy persists well into adulthood.
source: In some species of mammals, the influence of sex-steroids on MeA anatomy persists well into adulthood (Cooke et al., 1999) supporting our conclusion that additional hormone-dependent circuit changes occur after the perinatal organizational phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A multi-stage organizational model of sex-specific behavioral circuits is supported by elegant experiments in hamsters demonstrating profound rearrangements of circuits underlying social behaviors during puberty.
source: Moreover, a multi-stage organizational model of sex-specific behavioral circuits is supported by elegant experiments in hamsters demonstrating profound rearrangements of circuits underlying social behaviors during puberty (Zehr et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Death of MeA neurons during development is important for sculpting a sexually dimorphic circuit.
source: Death of MeA neurons during development is important for sculpting a sexually dimorphic circuit.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about MeA development.

claim: The functional properties of MeA units can be similar even though the number of cells in the male vs female MeA is different.
source: However, we now know that the functional properties of MeA units can be similar even though the number of cells in the male vs female MeA is different.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from juvenile mice showing similar responses despite anatomical differences.

claim: Synaptic input from the AOB to the MeA may be sculpted in adult mice to disproportionately favor AOB input carrying opposite sex information to the MeA.
source: Synaptic input from the AOB to the MeA may be sculpted in adult mice to disproportionately favor AOB input carrying opposite sex information to the MeA.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about possible mechanisms underlying the observed sexual dimorphism.

claim: Maturation of inhibition within the MeA at puberty may act to silence, or specifically shunt less robust MeA responses.
source: Alternatively, or in addition to, maturation of inhibition within the MeA at puberty may act to silence, or specifically shunt less robust MeA responses. This latter mechanism could act in a manner similar to the control of critical period plasticity within the cortex through a time- and steroid-dependent maturation of inhibitory connectivity (Hensch, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about possible mechanisms, supported by analogy to cited research on cortical development.

claim: The emergence of specific topographically segregated, and sexually dimorphic MeA responses indicate that the anatomical and functional processes by which response selectivity is achieved in the MeA do not act randomly.
source: The emergence of specific topographically segregated, and sexually dimorphic MeA responses indicate that the anatomical and functional processes by which response selectivity is achieved in the MeA do not act randomly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed organization of MeA responses.

claim: Specific circuit mechanisms yet to be uncovered must act together to allow features of vomeronasal information to be extracted from the overall AOB representation based on intrinsic MeA properties, as well as, the sex, age, and physiological status of the individual animal.
source: Rather, specific circuit mechanisms yet to be uncovered must act together to allow features of vomeronasal information to be extracted from the overall AOB representation based on intrinsic MeA properties, as well as, the sex, age, and physiological status of the individual animal.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms that remain to be discovered.

claim: The differences in MeA activity observed in males vs females, juveniles vs adults, or mutants vs wild-type animals correlate tightly with distinct patterns of social behaviors from each of these groups.
source: Remarkably, the differences in MeA activity observed in males vs females, juveniles vs adults, or mutants vs wild-type animals correlate tightly with distinct patterns of social behaviors from each of these groups.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed neural differences to known behavioral differences.

claim: The age- and sex-specific transformations in MeA sensory processing uncovered by this study are likely to underlie fundamental changes in social behavior throughout development.
source: This suggests that the age- and sex-specific transformations in MeA sensory processing uncovered by our study are likely to underlie fundamental changes in social behavior throughout development.
